concept.name: Time bar
concept.definition: A time bar is an OHLC(V) bar built by aggregating all trades within a fixed clock interval (1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day, etc.). It is the default sampling scheme in market data, in which bars are produced at uniform points in time regardless of how much trading occurred.
concept.intuition: Time bars chop the trading day into equal clock slices and summarize each slice — whether it contained three trades or three thousand.
concept.mechanics: Define a fixed interval Δt; group all ticks with timestamps in [t, t+Δt) and reduce to OHLCV. López de Prado notes that time bars oversample information-poor (quiet) periods and undersample information-rich (busy) periods, and exhibit serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, and non-normality of returns — motivating activity-based alternatives like tick, volume, and dollar bars.
concept.failure_modes: Statistical properties of time-bar returns (normality, homoskedasticity) are poor, which degrades many ML and econometric methods applied directly to them. Bars also align to arbitrary clock boundaries, splitting coherent bursts of activity.
concept.misconceptions: Uniform clock sampling does not produce uniform information sampling — a 1-minute bar at the open and one at lunch carry very different amounts of market information.
concept.example: A 1-minute time-bar series of EUR/USD produces 1,440 bars per day even though overnight bars may contain a handful of trades while London-open bars contain thousands.

citations.source: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018)
